title: The Hidden Lives of Teachers
author: Adam Robbins
summary: Adam Robbins builds on Graham Nuttall's The Hidden Lives of Learners, which identified three hidden worlds inside every classroom -- the teacher's world, the peer world, and the private world of the learner -- by proposing a fourth: the teacher's own hidden world of beliefs, values, and internal narratives. Developed through his Middle Leadership Mastery course, Robbins argues this fourth world explains why identical feedback or CPD can land completely differently depending on a teacher's prior experiences, confidence, and sense of professional identity. He argues effective CPD cannot simply present strategies; it must create space for reflection and coaching that surfaces teachers' hidden assumptions, and suggests Cognitive Coaching as one vehicle capable of doing this if delivered well.
points: Robbins' central move is extending Nuttall's three hidden worlds (teacher, peer, private/learner) with a fourth: the teacher's own hidden world of beliefs, values, and internal narratives, developed through his Middle Leadership Mastery course.
His concrete examples show how the same input lands differently depending on this hidden layer -- identical feedback can register as encouragement to one teacher and criticism to another.

The CPD design implication is explicit: presenting strategies alone can miss its mark; effective professional development needs reflection, discussion, or coaching that surfaces teachers' hidden assumptions.
Robbins points to Cognitive Coaching, delivered by knowledgeable practitioners, as a plausible mechanism for surfacing this fourth hidden world in practice.
quotes: One of his most enduring ideas is that beneath every classroom lie three hidden worlds. There is the teacher’s world, where lessons are carefully planned and delivered.
When I first began delivering my Middle Leadership Mastery course, I found myself adding a fourth hidden world: the teacher’s world of beliefs, values and internal narratives.
A piece of feedback might be heard as encouragement by one teacher, but as criticism by another.
If we ignore this hidden world, professional development can miss its mark. Leaders may deliver the same message, but teachers will interpret it in very different ways.
That is why effective CPD cannot just be about presenting strategies. It must also create space for reflection, discussion or coaching that surfaces the teacher’s hidden world.
It is in this world, of beliefs, values and interpretations, that the success of CPD is often decided.
